rv.q: Mr. Stewart's performance, strange though it may sound from time to time, is in the end both deeply comprehending and painfully touching, just like the play itself.

Hardships, petty humiliations, financial strain, crushed hopes: That's what you can expect as an actor. At least that's how it is in David Mamet's "A Life in the Theatre" -- and it's a comedy. The 1977 piece -- now being revived on Broadway under Neil Pepe's direction -- looks at two thespians' daily grind through a series of fast-paced vignettes.
Reader, have you noticed a whiff of misrule in the air? At home and abroad, terrorists and Tea Partiers, emboldened by ignorance, are threatening to bring an early fin to our siècle.
You can practically feel Patrick Stewart and T.R. Knight's joy in performing in the Broadway revival of David Mamet's 1977 'A Life in the Theatre.'
And in trying to look big, “A Life in the Theatre,” directed here by Neil Pepe, has never seemed smaller.

Stewart and Knight, both at the top of their game here, embrace the strange spirit of the show and imbue Mamet's 26 madcap vignettes with a feeling of buoyant, urgent comedy that elicits lots of laughs — and only the occasional grimace.
This kinder, gentler Mamet can be readily embraced in Neil Pepe's funny and bittersweet revival of A The Theatre.
If Stewart and Knight deftly manage the broad comedy required here, their overall performances are appropriately nuanced.
It takes a special talent to act this bad, and these guys raise it to the level of an art form.
Stars Patrick Stewart and T.R. Knight deliver brilliant comic performances in Neil Pepe's amusingly breezy production.

"A Life in the Theatre" is a rarity among David Mamet’s works. Rather than the usual corrosive vitriol against venal real-estate salesmen, corrupt politicians, racist lawyers, or profit-mad Hollywood types, this two-hander is a sweet valentine to the theater.
What is sorely lacking is a plot or character development, and certainly affection for the hapless actors which might enlist our empathy.
His actors, both accomplished individually, make no emotional connection.
Neil Pepe's directorial concept is pretty grand, and he's gotten Santo Loquasto to provide more set changes and Laura Bauer more costume pieces that your average Metropolitan Opera production.

If this ably staged, performed and designed production is not the most memorable show you will ever see, it certainly represents an agreeable time with a couple of excellent players exercising their craft.

cn.t: Critics offer mixed praise for this Mamet revival, applauding Stewart and Knight's chemistry and performances while questioning the play's slight substance and Pepe's overly elaborate production choices that slow the pace.
